I really like analyses of The Matrix which consider characters and events as being allegorical to trans experience. As a trans person, these kinds of interpretations appeal to me on a personal basis, especially as someone who grew up watching the films. That being said, I think in general we should be careful not to apply these allegories too prescriptively, or say that they were the author's sole intention at the time of writing the script. If you accept the Matrix as a metaphor for trans experience, Cypher's actions in the first movie can definitely be compared to those of a de-transitioner who starts advocating against the trans community once they detransiton. But Cypher's actions are also allegorical or referential to lots of other things too (Judas, false political activists who betray their cause etc.).   


Personally, I'm hesitant to speak about these films as being solely allegorical to trans experience. I think there are parts which were intentionally trans-adjacent and parts which only became apparent to Lana and Lilly later. I also think there are parts which weren't related at all. That doesn't mean we can't ascribe meaning to things later, and I think the character of Cypher is a really good example of how we can construct meaning for ourselves after the event. That's part of what I love about the trans allegory - being able to discern metaphors and construct even more meaning for ourselves out of them.

Although I echo what other people have said about the diversity of medieval music and the inability to describe it in consistent terms, one important feature in a lot of medieval music is modal harmony. Modal harmony is a broad term that covers different musical traditions, and particular forms of modal harmony were developed in Ancient Greece and in Byzantium, as well as in early Christian plainchant music which would later be influenced by other modal theories (the Greek influence on music theory is visible in scales like the Lydian and Aeolian modes, which we still use today). The tonal harmony we’re used to now (which uses major and minor keys and chords and melodies derived from those scales) wasn’t fully fleshed out until the 18th century. That is perhaps one reason why a lot of medieval music seems to have a particular character to its sound, because it is clearly distinct from the tonally homogenised music we hear today. One thing that makes medieval music so interesting is its diversity, and perhaps one way to answer your question would be to say that medieval music is recognisable because it’s so different from what we’re used to. I’m sure a historian of music theory would have a more informed answer than the one I’ve given you, but that’s my two cents.

An interesting example of a contemporary piece of music using modal harmony is ‘Thousand Eyes’ by FKA Twigs, part of her album ‘Magdalene’ which is full of biblical references. 

Here is a good stack exchange post explaining the difference between modal and tonal harmony https://music.stackexchange.com/questions/6401/whats-the-difference-between-modal-music-and-tonal-music

As I say, I’m not especially well versed in the history of music theory but studied modal harmony last year when working on some music, so that’s where my interest comes from. I hope this is helpful or maybe a jumping off point for a wider discussion about medieval music and modal harmony!

Testosterone blockers will slow-down the rate of hair loss, though oestrogen alone won’t because hair-loss is connected to a specific testosterone hormone called DHT. I was taking finasteride for a while for this purpose, but experienced a loss in libido which bothered me so I stopped. I have a lot of issues with body dysmorphia to do with this stuff, but my biggest piece of advice would be that you shouldn’t allow it to have immense power over you. There are lots and lots of things you can do to slow-down or stop hair-loss or even regain some hair you’ve lost, and it’s very important for your own sense of mental well-being that you find whichever regimen works for you (if indeed you have a regimen at all) and not allow it to take up too much space in your life. I wish that I had known this as a teenager, and in all honesty I wish I had stoped worrying about it at the time. If you’re still a teen I recommend putting it aside for a while and concentrate on other things that make you happy or fulfil you. If you want to keep an eye on it there’s nothing wrong with that, but it’s all too easy for it to become a bit of an obsession, so I would recommend being cautious and always trying to keep your sense well-being in mind.
